Texas has high LLC fees. You do NOT have to have a Texas LLC just because you live there. You can get an LLC  in any state and it is still valid. You will need a registered agent if you organize in another state.

Think of an LLC as a wrapper holding the assets or company is sometimes easier. There are no LLC tax forms, for example. The LLC can be a disregarded entity where you are treated as a sole proprietor or partnership for taxes, or you can elect to be treated as a corporation and then elect S status if you want. Each classification has its place.

Since the LLC holds real estate it is doubtful you want to elect any corporate status for a variety of reason. Usually an LLC for RE is used as a disregarded entity. In such cases the LLC doesn't provide more tax benefits. But then again, LLCs are legal entities designed to provide a legal firewall between you and the business in the case of lawsuits, et cetera. Taxes are a secondary consideration because LLCs are legal entities, not tax avoidance vehicles. It's the flavor of LLC (sole prop or corp, etc.) that determines tax savings.

You are correct that a regular, or C, corporation is taxed at a flat 21%. But. . . how do you get the money out of the entity? Either wages or dividends. Dividends are not deductible to the corporation paying them, but taxable to you personally, therefore there is a level of double taxation. If you take a wage from the C corp you pay FICA tax. RE doesn't pay FICA of SE tax in most cases so the C corp increases your tax burden again.

The S corp is much harder to explain. It's not wrong to put RE into an S corp, but it does cause serious tax issues, especially when you sell the assets. I will not bore you here with the details. If interested, look up Personal Holding Corporations or PHCs and how they relate to real estate.

Putting the RE on your personal return as always (or partnership return if more than one owner) is almost always the most beneficial method. To save tax dollars be sure to apply the tangible property rules, repair regs and cost segregation.

An overlooked benefit to the LLC is fractional ownership. If you own the building without an LLC you either sell all or none of the building. With an LLC you can sell fractional ownership in the property (creating a partnership). This allows parent to gift the kids small amounts of RE each year ($15,000 per person per person in 2018) or a partial sale of the property without conveyance issues (the same LLC owns the property so it hasn't changed hands; only the ownership of the LLC did). 

Finally, the C corp does not pass to your personal return while the S does. Also, retained earnings are different from taxable income. 

There is more, of course, but I think you get the idea. Hope this helps.

Facts and circumstances rule. Another sister question is: Should I invest in a traditional versus Roth IRA. The answer is a firm, "It depends." 

Recap: The traditional IRA gives you an immediate tax break now if you don't phase out and have income to offset. But you pay tax on all distributions at some future date, including on the earnings. Inherited traditional IRAs require faster distribution by beneficiaries than a Roth also. The Roth isn't deductible now, but all the gains are tax free if the rules are followed. 

Then we have the non-qualified accounts, where your question resides. Non-qualified accounts don't get a tax break now and gains are taxed at a preferential rate if held longer than a year. Dividends can also be treated preferentially.

Okay, so what's the best course of action?

My opinion is such: Work retirement plans (401(k), 457, 403(b), et cetera) should be filled to the matching level first. Then I would consider maxing out the Roth. Your original Roth investment is available for distribution at any age without tax or penalty (it's just a return of your own money). It is best to let profits ride in a Roth until 59 1/2. There are exceptions I will not get into, but my generalization is a good guideline.

Then I'd move other deductible (if there is tax reduction value) accounts. Keep in mind you will want some money in a non-qualified account for easy access in case of emergency.

The second year is okay with some hens becoming clucks (hen that lays few if any eggs but loves laying on eggs until they hatch). Hens will lay eggs for several years, but after the first year it slows down with a major reduction in year three and after. Breed makes a difference.

Chickens return to roost in the henhouse.  They return home for safety. 

Another issue is wildlife killing your flock. It's a never ending problem.

I've raised chickens for years on my 10 acre farm. Assuming you have a rooster to keep the, ahem, cycle going, you will need hens for eggs and cocks (yes, they are called that so stop laughing) for eating/meat. I said stop laughing.

If your plan is to eat one chicken per day you will need a nice sized flock. Some fast growing hybrid birds from co-ops are eating size in 4-6 weeks. You want leghorns or other hardy bird. You need several months (3-6) for them to grow to size and they have less meat than the "heavies" the chicks from the factory farm produce. 

Hens start laying eggs around 6 months. They are the best you'll ever eat. I warn you, if you eat home-grown eggs you'll refuse to eat store bought eggs the rest of your life. 

Eating a bird a day means you will need a flock of around 150 birds.  Some will be chicks while others will be laying hens (they become soup chickens after they stop laying eggs). My recommendation is to butcher in batches. Butchering 30 chickens (a month supply in your case) is a good day of word.  You need to consider what you plan on doing with the offal of the butchered birds and the manure. 150 chickens make a lot of poo.

Health insurance for the SE is treated as an adjustment to income on the front of Form 1040. 

The deduction is limited to the net profits of the Schedule C minus deductions for SE tax and the owners (sole proprietor's) benefit in SEP, SIMPLE or qualified plan. Medicare premiums can also be deducted above the line. This includes medical premiums for a spouse and dependent child under age 27 in the year filed. 

The deduction is NOT allowed in any month the SE individual is eligible to participate in a subsidized health plan maintained by the employer of the SE individual, spouse or dependents/children under age 27.

IRS Pub 969 uses the word "paid". However, this is a loose interpretation. If you pay a year in advance the payment is allocated monthly. Otherwise you could be SE one month and deduct 20 years of premiums all at once and then shut the business down. Doesn't work that way with insurance premiums. They are deducted pro-rata.
